essential: Sir James sends them to the Holyhead train at once; Tommy notes it is only the 24th, and Julius hurries them off.
Sir James regrets that a two o'clock meeting keeps him from coming; Julius is plainly glad to lose his company.
Julius produces his automatic, 'Little Willie', and boasts there is nobody to put Mr. Brown wise; Sir James answers with the Vandemeyer warning.
Sir James's parting advice: if they are shadowed, destroy the papers.
On the train Julius confesses he fell for Jane's photograph but was cured by the girl in the flesh, saying she is 'not like her photo one bit' though he recognised her.
Tommy coldly rebukes Julius for proposing to Tuppence within a fortnight; the 'businesslike' marriage exchange leaves Tommy heated, but he cools down before Holyhead.
They follow the gorse-lined path, and Tommy uneasily fancies someone is following them.
Julius is startled to find the begging-terrier boulder; Tommy affects British phlegm.
Tommy's outburst that the papers cannot be there after five years.
Julius pulls out the oilskin packet; Tommy remarks that the stitches look new.
Inside is a blank sheet; Julius guesses a dummy, Tommy guesses sympathetic ink, and heat over a twig fire brings out brown letters.
End on the printed message.

Julius arrives with the newspaper; Tommy explodes about his love for Tuppence and the nurse's kit.
Julius realises the nurse he saw at Bournemouth was 'Jane'; Tommy accuses her of being in with them, and Julius defends her patriotism.
Julius's anger vanishes abruptly; he calls himself an idiot and leaves for the London and North Western depot.
Tommy says 'I'm going to the devil' and has no plan beyond revenge.
Seeking writing paper in Julius's empty room, Tommy finds Annette's photograph in a drawer.

essential: The Prime Minister, harassed, asks whether things are less desperate; Carter shows Tommy's letter.

The letter's reasoning, in Tommy's boyish style: the Manchester girl and sham packet were a plant; Tommy thinks he knows the real Jane and where the papers are, and encloses his guess sealed, not to be opened till midnight on the 28th.
Tuppence's drowning was also a plant; the enemy will let Jane escape hoping she goes to the cache; knowledge of recovery would doom both girls; Tommy must reach Tuppence first.
The letter also requests a repeat of the telegram via Sir James and asks that the Soho house be watched day and night.
Carter keeps the envelope in the Bank vaults and refuses the PM's wish to open it, because Tommy trusted him.
Carter characterises Tommy as slow, unimaginative and tenacious, Tuppence as intuitive: 'Pace and stamina'.
Carter senses Peel Edgerton working in the dark, and reports Sir James's request about the disfigured unidentified body found near the New York docks.
Sir James arrives; the PM thinks 'My successor, perhaps!'.
Sir James recounts Tommy's phone call: the photograph in Hersheimmer's drawer bore a Californian photographer's mark, its original was Annette, and Tommy put it back.
Sir James suggested the telegram was altered; Carter reads the original; the overlooked clue was the page-boy's 'Charing Cross'.
Sir James says Tommy is at Gatehouse; he is 'preparing a case', knows who the dead American was but cannot prove it, and answers the photograph question with 'Perhaps it never left it'.
Julius returns two days later and finds Tommy's Argentine farewell note; he smiles and throws it away.
optional: The PM's whimsical 'successor' thought can be cut if space is tight.
The 'busy on a case'/'holiday' banter can be compressed while keeping 'preparing a case'.
The 'Inspector Brown' interjection and Sir James's exit line can be shortened.
risks: Sir James's gentle insinuation must read as plausibly helpful.

essential: Tommy enlists Albert at South Audley Mansions; Albert's 'Underworld' comic misunderstanding; the dying-aunt excuse; they meet at Charing Cross.
At the Gatehouse inn the landlord describes Astley Priors' Dr. Adams as genial, popular and keeping 'balmy' private patients; Tommy doubts, and no one recognises Tuppence or Annette.
First night: Albert's comic crawling; the dinner party talking cricket; Tommy's cold uncertainty.
Albert, disguised as the greengrocer's boy, learns a French young lady is staying in the house.
It is the 27th and Labour Day is the 29th; Tommy's understanding of the stakes, and his belief that capturing Brown would collapse everything.
Tommy kept the envelope sealed as bait; he is aghast at his presumption yet persists.
Tuppence's silhouette at a second-floor window; Tommy sings the hospital song while drunk-acting; the butler and footman eject him, and the butler is Whittington.
Albert brings back 'To-morrow--same time' and confesses his frog-croak message; Tommy reasons he is a pawn allowed to proceed.
At noon a carter delivers a note in Tuppence's hand: don't come tonight, they are being taken to Wales/Holyhead, Annette told her of his escape; signed 'Twopence'.
Tommy orders packing, then halts it on rereading, and declares he knows who the other fool is.
